Utilities costs of £7,890 were £610 below budget. This is largely due to a mild winter and the installation of a more efficient boiler in the clubhouse in March 2024 (cost £3,200, capitalised). Gas usage fell by 12% compared to 2023. Electricity usage was broadly flat. Water charges increased by 4% in line with the regional tariff.

**3.5 Repairs & Maintenance**

Repairs and maintenance totalled £8,940, which was £1,440 over budget. The overspend relates to emergency repairs to the clubhouse roof following storm damage in October (cost £2,150, not covered by insurance due to the excess) and replacement of the main gate lock after a break-in attempt (£180). The summer months (June to August) remain the busiest, reflecting the higher level of match, training and social activity on the pitches and in the clubhouse. We also negotiated a small discount with our main drinks wholesaler in March, which applied to the bulk of our orders for the rest of the year.

Stock levels at the year end were £1,340, which is in line with our normal holding and represents approximately two weeks of sales at the December rate. The seasonal pattern of bar sales is well established and the 2024 figures follow the usual shape, with a clear peak in the summer. The winter months (November to February) are quieter, and we deliberately hold lower stock levels during this period to avoid tying up cash and to reduce the risk of wastage. The main exception is December, when we build up stock for the Christmas social events.

We have a standing order with the wholesaler for the core draught lines, which is adjusted each month based on the previous year's sales for the same month and the forecast of upcoming events. This worked well in 2024, with only two occasions where we ran out of a popular line (a lager in July and a cider in August). - Replacement of the four existing floodlight columns with six new LED columns.
- Installation of a new control system to allow dimming and remote switching.
- Estimated cost of £38,000, including installation and disposal of the old columns.
- Proposed timeline: works to commence in May 2025 and complete by August 2025, ahead of the winter season.

- **Installation costs:** Cole & Sons, the preferred contractor, had provided a firm quotation of £12,800 for installation and electrical works, which was £800 higher than the initial estimate. This was due to the need for additional groundworks around the base of the new columns and the requirement to isolate the power supply during the works.
- **Supply costs:** The supplier had confirmed a price increase of £400 on the LED fittings, effective from 1 October. If the order was placed before that date, the original price would be honoured.
- **Structural engineering:** The structural engineer had submitted a revised invoice for £3,650, reflecting additional time spent on the design of the column foundations.

She noted that the Club's capital reserves were sufficient to cover the shortfall, but she recommended that the Board consider options to reduce the forecast.

He proposed removing the remote switching function and retaining only the dimming capability. This would still deliver the energy savings identified in the lighting survey. Anita asked whether this would affect the youth teams' use of the lights. Darren confirmed that dimming would still allow the lights to be set to a lower level for training, and that remote switching was a convenience feature rather than a requirement.

She reminded the Board that the grant application had been submitted in June and that the foundation had indicated a decision would be made within three months. 11. Constitutional Amendments

The Chair explained that the committee had proposed two amendments to the Club's constitution, which had been circulated to members in advance of the meeting. The first amendment related to the quorum required for committee meetings, and the second related to the procedure for calling an EGM.

The first amendment was proposed that the quorum for committee meetings be reduced from five to four, to ensure that meetings could still go ahead during holiday periods when officers might be away. This was seconded by D. Whitfield. There was some discussion about whether this would make it easier for decisions to be made without full representation, but the majority of members present felt that four was a reasonable number given the size of the committee. The amendment was put to the vote and carried with 24 votes in favour and 3 against.

The second amendment was proposed that the notice period for an EGM be reduced from twenty-one days to fourteen days, to allow the committee to respond more quickly to urgent matters. This was seconded by L. Nguyen. A member asked whether this would give members enough time to prepare, and the Chair confirmed that fourteen days was still a reasonable period and that the committee had no intention of calling EGMs without good reason. The amendment was put to the vote and carried unanimously.

The Chair confirmed that both amendments would take effect immediately and that the constitution would be updated accordingly. A copy of the revised constitution would be made available on the Club website.

documents.content:
Total takings were **£34,290**, an increase of **6.0%** on the 2023 figure of £32,350. This was £1,290 ahead of the budget of £33,000 set at the start of the year. The increase was fairly consistent across the year, with no single month showing an exceptional spike. The summer months (June to August) remain the busiest, reflecting the higher level of match, training and social activity on the pitches and in the clubhouse. December takings were stronger than expected, helped by the Christmas quiz night and the annual members' social, both of which were well attended.

**4.2 Cost of Sales**

The cost of goods sold for the bar was **£17,220**, compared to £16,940 in 2023. The gross profit margin was therefore **49.8%** in 2024, slightly down from 47.6% in 2023. The improvement in margin is largely due to a change in the mix of products sold: draught lager and cider accounted for a higher proportion of sales than in 2023, and these lines carry a higher margin than bottled products. We also negotiated a small discount with our main drinks wholesaler in March, which applied to the bulk of our orders for the rest of the year.

Stock levels at the year end were £1,340, which is in line with our normal holding and represents approximately two weeks of sales at the December rate. No stock write-offs were required, although a small amount of out-of-date soft drink stock (approx. £40) was disposed of in September. The cellar was re-ordered in November and a full stock-take was carried out on 31 December; the count agreed with the book stock to within £15, which was treated as shrinkage.

**4.3 Bar Profit**

The treasurer's report shows Ashworth Vale Community Sports Club bar_profit_2024 as 5670 GBP. Record status: historical.

The bar made a profit of **£5,670** for the year. This is the figure that will be carried into the income and expenditure account for 2024 and is the final, audited figure for the year. The profit is £1,020 higher than in 2023 (£4,650) and is £670 above the budget of £5,000. The improvement reflects both the higher takings and the better gross margin, offset by a small increase in bar wages (see below) and the cost of the annual cellar inspection.

Bar wages, which are included in the staffing costs shown in section 3.6 of this report, were £8,120 for the bar specifically. This is an increase of £410 on 2023, reflecting the rise in the National Living Wage in April and the fact that we employed an additional part-time bar assistant for the summer months. Bar wages as a percentage of bar takings fell from 24.7% to 23.7%, which shows that the additional hours were more than covered by the extra sales.

**4.4 Seasonal Variations and Stock Management**

The seasonal pattern of bar sales is well established and the 2024 figures follow the usual shape, with a clear peak in the summer. The winter months (November to February) are quieter, and we deliberately hold lower stock levels during this period to avoid tying up cash and to reduce the risk of wastage. The main exception is December, when we build up stock for the Christmas social events.

We have a standing order with the wholesaler for the core draught lines, which is adjusted each month based on the previous year's sales for the same month and the forecast of upcoming events. This worked well in 2024, with only two occasions where we ran out of a popular line (a lager in July and a cider in August). In both cases, a delivery was arranged within two working days and the loss of sales was minimal. The Finance Sub-committee has asked me to note that the recent price increases from the breweries have not yet been passed on in full to members, and that a review of bar prices will be undertaken in early 2025. Any price change will be proposed to the Committee before being implemented.

Darren confirmed that dimming would still allow the lights to be set to a lower level for training, and that remote switching was a convenience feature rather than a requirement.

Ruth noted that the Football Foundation grant decision was still expected by the end of September. If the grant was successful, a proportion of the costs would be covered, which would reduce the pressure on Club reserves. She reminded the Board that the grant application had been submitted in June and that the foundation had indicated a decision would be made within three months. No further update had been received as of the meeting date.

Priya proposed that the Board approve a revised total budget of £40,000, with the £2,000 increase to be funded from Club reserves if the grant was unsuccessful. She noted that this would be subject to final confirmation of the grant outcome. Martin seconded the proposal.

**Action 3.1:** Ruth to contact the Football Foundation on 17 September to request an update on the grant decision. *Owner: Ruth Okafor. Due: 20 September 2024.*

**Action 3.2:** Darren to obtain a revised quotation from the control system supplier for a simplified specification (dimming only, no remote switching). *Owner: Darren Cole. Due: 20 September 2024.*

**CLUBHOUSE EXTENSION PROJECT – MEETING MINUTES**

**Meeting No:** 14  
**Date:** 24 September 2024

**Venue:** Clubhouse Committee Room  
**Chair:** Priya Sharma (Project Sponsor)  
**Attendees:** Martin Bell (Project Manager), Anita Desai (Club Secretary), Ruth Okafor (Finance), Darren Cole (Facilities), Tom Whitfield (Contractor PM, APEX Build), James Oyelaran (Structural Engineer, via phone)  
**Apologies:** None

---

**1. Actions from Previous Meeting**

| Ref | Action | Owner | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3.1 | Contact Football Foundation re grant decision | Ruth | **Closed** – update received, see item 6 |
| 3.2 | Revised quotation for simplified lighting control spec | Darren | **Closed** – quotation received, see item 4 |

---

**2. Contractor Update – APEX Build**

Tom Whitfield reported that the steel frame erection for the new clubhouse extension was completed on 19 September, two days ahead of schedule. The roof trusses are now being installed and the team expects the roof to be watertight by 8 October, weather permitting. The external blockwork to the east elevation will start next week.

Tom raised a concern regarding the delivery of the glazing units. The supplier, FenGlass Ltd, has advised that the bespoke double-glazed units for the main hall will be delayed by approximately 10 working days. This is due to a production issue at their factory. The revised delivery date is 21 October. Tom has asked his procurement officer to investigate alternative suppliers, but he cautioned that a like-for-like replacement would be difficult to source at short notice given the bespoke specification.

The Board discussed the impact of this delay. Martin noted that the glazing is on the critical path for the internal fit-out. If the units arrive on 21 October, the fit-out would be delayed by about one week. This would push the practical completion date from 15 December to approximately 22 December. The Clubhouse is normally used for the Christmas Eve family event, and Anita asked whether the delay would affect that booking.

Tom confirmed that the main hall would be usable for the event even if the internal fit-out was not fully complete. He noted that the temporary power supply would be sufficient for lighting and heating, and that the kitchen would not be affected as it is in the existing building. The Board noted this assurance.

**Decision 14.1:** The Board accepted the revised glazing delivery date of 21 October and agreed that the practical completion target would be revised to 22 December 2024. Martin to update the project programme accordingly.

---

**3. Change Request – CR-009 (Kitchen Ventilation)**

Ruth presented Change Request CR-009, which had been circulated by email on 18 September. The request relates to the upgrading of the kitchen ventilation system in the existing building. The current system is undersized for the planned catering capacity of the new clubhouse. The original specification included a standard extraction unit, but the Club’s caterer has confirmed that a more powerful unit is required to meet the expected demand.

The additional cost is £4,200, which includes the unit, ducting, and installation. The project contingency fund currently stands at £6,500, so the cost can be met from contingency without requiring additional funding.

James Oyelaran confirmed that the structural implications of the upgrade are minimal. The new unit will be mounted on the external wall, and the existing opening for the current unit can be reused. He recommended that the work be carried out at the same time as the main roof works to avoid scaffolding costs later.

**Decision 14.2:** The Board approved Change Request CR-009 at a cost of £4,200, to be funded from the project contingency. Ruth to update the budget register.
